PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let's talk about PL1M. This transformer is part of a site that has already made a real commitment to energy field correction. MPTS assets are deployed and working. The reactive burden has been addressed — at least partially — and the field is in a better state than it was before that investment was made. That matters, and it should be acknowledged. Here's where we are right now with PL1M specifically. When I go to pull the numbers — the tuned baseline readings, the voltage profile, the reactive load figures, the thermal burden, the savings projection — I'm coming up empty on both sides. The Mercury CSV analysis returned null values across the board, and the image data for the view sequence — that's the voltage view, the tuned baseline target, the measurement view, and the savings projection — none of it came through for this transformer. So what I can tell you with confidence is the structure of what we need to complete this picture. We need the kVAR maximum from the tuned baseline target view to confirm whether the installed assets are sized correctly for the current load profile. We need the voltage waveform from the tuned voltage view to check whether the field is holding near 480 volts or still showing stress dips. And we need the savings view to measure the optimization gap — the distance between where the tuned field sits today and where it can perform with full correction. The good news is that PL1M's analysis framework is completely ready. The moment that data comes back in, we can quantify exactly what the installed investment has already recovered — in dollars, in heat burden, in cooling overhead — and identify any incremental refinement that would close the remaining gap. That's how we protect the investment already made. That's the Unity standard.

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
PL1M is part of a tuned site — MPTS assets are in place, and the field is already benefiting from reactive correction. That investment is real and it's working. For this analysis pass, however, PL1M came back with no data — neither the Mercury CSV nor the image views for this transformer were available. That means I can't give you the power factor reading, the reactive load in kVAR, the thermal burden in BTU per hour, or the optimization gap between the tuned baseline and the savings target. All of those are value unavailable until the data is resubmitted. What I can tell you is that once those numbers come in, this analysis will immediately tell you two things: how much of the original waste has already been captured by the installed assets, and whether there's a meaningful remaining gap worth addressing through incremental refinement. No new deployment recommendations — just honest measurement of where the tuned field stands and where it can go. Resubmit the view package for PL1M and we'll complete the picture.

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me walk you through PL1M in full detail — because even when the data isn't there, understanding the framework tells you exactly what to look for and why it matters. PL1M is operating in what we call tuned-field optimization mode. That means this isn't a site that's sitting on uncorrected reactive burden and wondering what to do about it. This is a site that made a decision, committed to MPTS correction, installed the equipment, and is now in the phase where the work is about refinement, measurement, and stewardship — not first deployment. That distinction is important. In a tuned field, the conversation shifts. We're not asking whether you should invest in correction. That answer came earlier, and the investment was made. Now we're asking something more precise: how much of the original problem has been solved, and how much opportunity remains on the table? The tool we use to answer that is the optimization gap — the measured distance between the tuned baseline target, which we call TBT, and the tuned savings projection, which we call TS. The TBT view shows the field as it currently operates with the installed assets running. The TS view shows where the field can perform when correction is dialed in to its designed capacity. The gap between those two views — in kilowatt-hours recovered, in kVAR suppressed, in BTU per hour of heat burden lifted, in dollars per year of cooling overhead reduced — that gap is the remaining optimization opportunity. For PL1M specifically, I need to be direct with you. Both data streams came back empty for this transformer in this analysis pass. The Mercury CSV returned null values — zero power factor, zero kVA target, zero kVAR maximum. The image views for the voltage profile, the tuned baseline, the measurement window, and the savings projection — none of them were available for extraction. That creates a complete numeric blackout for PL1M. I cannot tell you the peak demand in kilowatts. I cannot tell you the supply target in kVA. I cannot characterize whether the voltage profile is holding near the 480-volt nominal or showing repeated dips that indicate residual field stress. I cannot quantify the thermal burden in BTU per hour or the cooling cost in dollars per hour. And I cannot measure the TBT-to-TS optimization gap that would tell you whether the installed assets are fully closing the reactive correction window or leaving measurable recovery on the table. What I can tell you is what the engineering attention areas look like when that data arrives. First, voltage stability. In a tuned field, the voltage waveform should be holding close to nominal. If the TV view shows triangular dips, sustained sags, or gold vertical streaks — which indicate power-off intervals — those are signals that the correction point may need adjustment or that load patterns have shifted since commissioning. Second, reactive load adequacy. The kVAR maximum from TBT gets divided by 400 to determine how many H490 units the field needs. If the installed count falls short of that number, residual reactive burden is expected and quantifiable. Third, the savings projection from TS. That header will show recovered power factor — targeting 99.5 percent — along with estimated annual savings, heat burden relief, and cooling cost recovery. Those numbers, compared against the TBT baseline, tell the complete story of optimization progress. The moment PL1M's image and CSV data come back in, this analysis completes immediately. The framework is built. The questions are defined. The comparison structure is ready. Until then, PL1M is marked as a data-gap transformer in the group site overview. It will not contribute numeric values to site-level totals or averages. That's the right call — clean data produces clean decisions. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard.

In a tuned field, the MPTS assets are actively suppressing reactive demand, and the TBT (tuned baseline target) view is the key reference for understanding how much reactive burden remains after correction. The TS (tuned savings) view then shows the projected outcome if the field reaches its optimized state — the gap between TBT and TS is the remaining opportunity.

Every degree of excess heat shortens insulation life, increases the risk of a thermal event, and forces cooling systems to run harder. In a tuned-field environment, the goal of MPTS correction is to reduce that stress load — to bring the transformer closer to its designed operating point and let the insulation and cooling infrastructure operate within their comfort zones.

For PL1M, the thermal burden figures — measured in BTU per hour — are unavailable from both image and CSV sources. The cooling cost overlay, which would show the kilowatt load and hourly cost of compensating for excess heat, is similarly unavailable. Without these values, I cannot quantify the stress reduction that the installed MPTS assets have already achieved for PL1M, nor can I characterize the residual stress that remains in the optimized field gap.

What I can tell you structurally is this: in tuned-field optimization mode, the thermal story has two chapters. Chapter one is the reduction already achieved — the difference between the original untuned field and the current TBT state. Chapter two is the remaining optimization gap — the further thermal relief that would come from closing the distance between TBT and TS. Both chapters require live numeric data to tell properly. PL1M's operational stress section is ready to receive those values and will be completed as soon as image and CSV data are available.
